newsitem.title: LIBERIA: Liberia extends voter registration for key poll.
newsitem.headline: Liberia extends voter registration for key poll.

text.p: Authorities in Liberia gave more time on Monday for people to register to vote in July 19 elections wrapping up a transition from years of civil war.

But as the elections commission announced the three-day extension for voters in rural areas, political parties alleging irregularities called a meeting for Tuesday to push for a postponement of the poll.
Officials of 12 of 13 parties contesting the presidential and parliamentary elections held consultations on Monday ahead of the meeting at which they expect to suggest a new poll date.
"I understand they are working on a document that will include all the concerns we are raising," said Kona Khasu, an aide to Ellen Johnson-Sirleaf, the only woman in the presidential race.

Other sources said the parties were struggling to find a common ground on the question of how long the elections should be delayed if their calls were accepted by Liberia's West African peace brokers.

"If you were to ask me my opinion, I would say we don't want any postponement," Milton Teajay, an official of the United People's Party, told Reuters. "There were minor frauds and to prevent them from being massive, we must go ahead with these elections as planned."
Presidential front-runner Charles Taylor opposes a delay.

Many Liberians fear that controversy over the election date could plunge the West African nation, founded in 1847 by freed American slaves, into renewed conflict after a delicately negotiated accord to end seven years of civil war.
Representatives of the parties, except for Taylor's National Patriotic Front of Liberia, called for the postponement at meetings on Friday and Saturday.

"There was a general consensus in the meeting that elections be delayed because there are frauds in the process leading up to the elections," said Cletus Wotorson, the presidential candidate of the Alliance Party.
Nevertheless many candidates intensified their campaign in the interior while party leaders argued over the poll date.
Western diplomats whose governments are helping fund the poll have cautioned about donor fatigue, and may still be able to exert some leverage to ensure the election stays on course.

The peace plan brokered by the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) scheduled the poll and set the swearing in of an elected president for August 2, if a winner emerges with more than 50 percent of the votes.
Taylor, who launched a civil war in December 1989 and is confident of winning the presidential election, is pressing ahead with campaigning.
In addition to Taylor and Boley, a third powerful warlord -- Alhaji Kromah of the mainly Moslem Mandigo ULIMO party -- is running for the presidency.
Johnson-Sirleaf, a former United Nations official and a one-time cabinet minister, is widely rated as the most serious civilian contender.
The electoral commission said it was impressed with the turnout of voters during registration but gave no figures.

"Registration is extended in the rural areas because the exercise began there very late," commission spokesman Momo Kanneh said. "There were allegations of frauds and other irregularities but they were minor. The exercise was generally credible."
